title: Modal Verbs (can, should, must)
simpleExplanation: Modal verbs express ability (can), advice (should), or obligation (must). Followed by base verb without 'to'.
detailedExplanation: Modals: can (ability), could (past ability/polite request), should (advice), must (strong obligation), may/might (possibility), would (conditional/polite). Never add -s for third person. Main verb stays in base form without 'to'. Negatives: cannot/can't, shouldn't, mustn't. Questions: invert modal and subject.
usage: I can swim. | You should study. | We must go.
avoidWhen: Don't add -to after modals (not 'can to swim').
simpleExplanation_en: Modal verbs express ability (can), advice (should), or obligation (must). Followed by base verb without 'to'.
simpleExplanation_id: Modal menyatakan kemampuan (can), saran (should), atau keharusan (must). Diikuti kata kerja dasar tanpa to.
detailedExplanation_en: Modals: can (ability), could (past ability/polite request), should (advice), must (strong obligation), may/might (possibility), would (conditional/polite). Never add -s for third person. Main verb stays in base form without 'to'. Negatives: cannot/can't, shouldn't, mustn't. Questions: invert modal and subject.
detailedExplanation_id: Modal: can (bisa), could (bisa lampau/permohonan sopan), should (saran), must (keharusan kuat), may/might (kemungkinan), would (kondisional/sopan). Tidak pernah tambah -s untuk orang ketiga. Kata kerja utama tetap dasar.
usage_en: I can swim. | You should study. | We must go.
usage_id: I can swim. | You should study. | We must go.
avoidWhen_en: Don't add -to after modals (not 'can to swim').
avoidWhen_id: Jangan tambah to setelah modal (bukan can to swim).

title: Comparative and Superlative Adjectives
pattern: big → bigger → biggest | more beautiful → most beautiful
simpleExplanation: Short adjectives add -er/-est. Long adjectives use more/most. Use 'than' with comparatives.
detailedExplanation: One-syllable adjectives: add -er/-est (tall→taller→tallest). Two syllables ending in -y: change -y to -ier/-iest (happy→happier→happiest). Longer adjectives: use more/most (beautiful→more beautiful→most beautiful). Irregular: good→better→best, bad→worse→worst. Use 'than' for comparisons. Superlatives need 'the'.
usage: She is taller than me. | This is the best book.

title: Present Perfect Tense
simpleExplanation: Present perfect links past and present. Use for experiences, unfinished time, and results now.
detailedExplanation: Form: have/has + past participle. Uses: (1) life experiences without specific time (I have visited Paris), (2) actions in unfinished time periods (today, this week), (3) recent past with present result (He has lost his keys - he can't open the door now). Often with: ever, never, already, yet, just, for, since. Don't use with specific past time.
usage: I have lived here for 5 years. | She has just arrived.
avoidWhen: Don't use with specific past time (yesterday, last year).

examples.text: Have you ever been to London?

title: Conditional Sentences (Zero & First)
pattern: If + present, present | If + present, will + base verb
simpleExplanation: Zero conditional for general truths (if + present, present). First conditional for real future possibilities (if + present, will + verb).
detailedExplanation: Zero conditional: If + present simple, present simple. For facts and general truths (If you heat water to 100°C, it boils). First conditional: If + present simple, will + base verb. For real future possibilities (If it rains tomorrow, I will stay home). 'If' clause can come first or second. Use comma when 'if' clause is first.
usage: If you study, you learn. | If I see her, I'll tell her.
avoidWhen: Don't use 'will' in the if-clause for first conditional.

examples.text: If you press this button, the light turns on.
